title: Pilot latency retro + next-tuning plan
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on TTFT reductions and streaming stability. Reviewed last week's benchmark logs, hypothesized kernel/scheduling causes for 95th percentile spikes, agreed on three tuning experiments (shorter max sequence cap, adaptive streaming chunks, force int8 kernels for older GPUs). Action: Redwood to deliver per-request KV metrics and a patched kernel config; BluePeak to provide representative production prompt mixes and a sample trace. Next meeting scheduled in 7 days to review experiment results.
next_steps: Redwood to upload experimental kernel config and autoscaler hints by 2025-09-12
BluePeak to share 3-day production prompt sample and token distribution by 2025-09-11
Schedule 1-hour follow-up to review metrics on 2025-09-16
action_items: Samir Patel: Post the 'ttft-experiments' kernel.cfg and runbook to shared folder (due 2025-09-12)
Leah Kim: Enable request-level KV payload logging on the pilot cluster and send sample traces (due 2025-09-12)
Maya Chen: Provide real prompt mix zip + avg seq histogram (due 2025-09-11)
Oliver Grant: Capture a 30-min flamegraph during a 95th pct spike window and upload (due 2025-09-14)
Priya Rao: Add a dashboard tile for per-request cold-start count and streaming rebuffer events (due 2025-09-13)
transcript:
[00:00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): Okay everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll pick up where we left off on the TTFT experiments.
[00:00:10] Javier (BluePeak): Hey Samir, Maya, Oliver, Nina here. All good.
[00:00:18] Leah (Redwood SE): Hi. I pulled the logs from the last 72 hours and there are a couple of patterns I want to highlight before we dig in.
[00:00:28] Maya (BluePeak): Sorry, just a quick note, we saw a production blip yesterday around 11:30 where the stream stalled for a few seconds — might be useful.
[00:00:36] Samir: Yes, that's one of the things we correlated to the 95th percentile TTFT spikes. Leah, you want to start with what you found?
[00:00:45] Leah: Sure. So quick framing: baseline was the dedicated pilot cluster with mixed p4/p40-ish capacity, models running in fp16. We saw average TTFT around 160ms but 95th was up to 1.2s in the busiest hour. Two main hypotheses: one, large sequence requests (250–400 tokens) trigger KV cache rehydration and chunked kernel paths which increase dispatch latency; two, streaming backpressure — small writes and flushing behavior cause extra scheduler hops.
[00:01:15] Oliver (BluePeak SRE): Can you explain chunked kernel path — I thought kernels were per-layer and unchanged by seq len?
[00:01:22] Leah: Good question. The runtime picks specialized kernels for long sequence windows and for certain attention patterns; when we hit a threshold we fall back to an alternate path that serializes some ops and increases CPU-GPU syncs. It's subtle, but we can see it in the traces — there's an extra 80–200ms hop between token 1 and token 2 for those cases.
[00:01:42] Maya: That matches our symptoms — initial token comes fast then second token arrives late, and the stream front-end reports a stall.
[00:01:50] Samir: Okay, so mapping to fixes: Leah suggested three short experiments — cap max sequence per request to 192, try adaptive streaming chunk sizes (send 32 then 64), and force int8 kernels on older GPUs to reduce kernel dispatch cost.
[00:02:07] Leah: Yeah. I'll add that forcing int8 is lower precision but our early evals showed negligible quality hit with the BluePeak prompts. The win is fewer bytes moved and smaller kernel launch overhead.
[00:02:18] Javier: Quick pushback — int8 on our datasets might regress on named entities, we need to validate.
[00:02:25] Maya: Agreed. We'll run a 1k prompt regression set if you push int8.
[00:02:30] Samir: Perfect. Leah, can you walk us through the patched kernel config you mentioned?
[00:02:35] Leah: Yes, I pushed a branch — it's basically three toggles. One: max_seq_cap=192 applied at the request router so requests are auto-resharded; two: streaming_chunk_policy=adaptive with initial_chunk=32; three: kernel_prefer_int8=on for devices that report compute capability < 8.0. There's also an optional kv_prefetch=aggressive flag we can toggle.
[00:02:58] Oliver: What does auto-resharding look like in practice? If a 500-token prompt comes in, do you split into multiple model passes?
[00:03:05] Leah: We rewrite the request as a prefix+continuation split. The runtime can keep KV across the split if the client is in the same session; if not, we may have to materialize partial KV which costs. We're trying to avoid expensive materialize paths.
[00:03:18] Maya: That materialize path is exactly what triggered spikes last week.
[00:03:22] Samir: Noted. Priya, did you finish adding the per-request KV metric hooks?
[00:03:27] Priya (Observability): I started — there's a PR that exposes kv_hits/kv_misses and cold_start boolean per request via tracing. It's on staging, I'll promote to pilot after we agree.
[00:03:36] Javier: Good. We really need to see cold_start counts correlated to TTFT.
[00:03:40] Leah: We'll add a dashboard tile for that.
[00:03:43] [00:03:43] (05:00 into meeting, sampling jump in transcript — transcription picked up "mm-hmm")
[00:04:02] Leah: From the nightly traces, many of the 95th pct cases are correlated with requests that have heavy prompt expansions — think long context retrieval then prompt concat — so the model enters a slightly different attention path.
[00:04:20] Maya: Is there a way to precompute or cache those long prefixes?
[00:04:24] Leah: Yes, prefix caching is an option. We can cache common prefixes at the router and serve them as a single tokenized state to avoid repeated re-tokenization and KV warmup. But cache hit rates depend on prompt variability.
[00:04:36] Oliver: Our prompt variety is high — we're worried cache won't cover enough.
[00:04:40] Samir: That's why we'll run the experiments in parallel: sequence cap, streaming chunk adaptation, and int8 kernel toggles, plus a light prefix-cache trial. We'll instrument everything.
[00:04:51] [00:04:51] Maya: Timeline?
[00:04:53] Samir: Leah, propose how long each experiment will run.
[00:04:56] Leah: I'd say a 48–72 hour window per experiment to capture peak diurnal patterns; we can overlap if we isolate by traffic buckets. For example, run int8 on 20% of replica pool, run seq cap on 30% request-routes, and prefix-cache only on a low-risk customer subset.
[00:05:13] Javier: Can you do that without impacting SLOs? We need rollbacks to be instant.
[00:05:18] Leah: Rollbacks are fast — we can toggle kernel_prefer_int8 at runtime and drain back to fp16. The only sticky case is if materialize path created expired cache entries; we'll clear those.
[00:05:29] Priya: Also adding an automated fallback: if TTFT > 800ms for 3 consecutive minutes on experiment cohort, system flips that cohort back to default.
[00:05:38] Samir: Good safety net.
[00:05:40] Oliver: About streaming chunking — you said initial_chunk=32 then 64, why that progression?
[00:05:45] Leah: The idea is to prioritize early latency: smaller first chunk gives faster first tokens, then larger chunks amortize kernel overhead for the rest. We also adjust flush intervals to avoid tiny writes causing backpressure.
[00:06:00] Maya: Will that increase overall bandwidth?
[00:06:02] Leah: Slightly, but network isn't the bottleneck in our traces; it's GPU dispatch latency.
[00:06:06] [00:06:06] Samir: Quick note on observability: Leah, can you add a trace label that marks which experiment flags were active for each request?
[00:06:13] Leah: Yep, experiment_flags is part of the trace header.
[00:06:16] Maya: About the kernel selection — can you force the newer fused-kernel path for certain layers? We've seen fused kernels help on similar models.
[00:06:25] Leah: We can, but fused kernels are sensitive to model op shapes; they may not be safe across all layers. We can force fused for attention layers only and run a short correctness pass.
[00:06:35] Javier: Sounds risky; how long for the correctness pass?
[00:06:37] Leah: A few hours with the regression set.
[00:06:40] [00:06:40] Samir: Let's schedule that as a pre-step for the int8 experiment.
[00:06:43] Priya: Also, I'll add a regression alert that fails the experiment if perplexity or exact-match drops beyond threshold.
[00:06:50] Maya: For our internal validation we will run named-entity recall and a small human spot check.
[00:06:55] Oliver: Do we have cost implications if we force int8 vs fp16?
[00:06:59] Leah: int8 generally lowers GPU memory and allows denser packing, so cost per token drops. But there's an engineering cost for monitoring and rollback guardrails. We'll estimate delta after we run.
[00:07:10] Samir: Ok moving on — Jon, you had a note about scheduler queueing in the kernel.
[00:07:14] Jon (PS): Yeah, small item: we've seen some contention in the host-side scheduler when many small streaming writes occur; the scheduler admission window is tuned for larger batches. My proposal is to adjust the scheduler to batch small streaming writes for a 5–10ms window to reduce overhead. There's a tradeoff with latency but a small wait improves throughput and reduces dispatch calls.
[00:07:34] Oliver: That could help the 95th pct if it's the host scheduler causing the hop.
[00:07:38] Leah: We'll add a 5ms batching config to the pilot host scheduler and run a micro-benchmark.
[00:07:43] Maya: Could that add jitter to our streaming? Users expect smooth token flow.
[00:07:47] Leah: The initial chunk remains immediate; this only batches subsequent tiny writes.
[00:07:52] [00:07:52] (break in transcript, faint cross-talk)
[00:08:05] Samir: Let's capture the specific metrics we need to evaluate success. Prioritized: median TTFT, 95th TTFT, streaming stall count, cold_start rate, kv_miss rate, and a small quality metric (NER F1 on regression set).
[00:08:20] Priya: Affirmative, I'll wire those into the pilot dashboard and share permalinks.
[00:08:23] Maya: For quality we also want token-level diff on a safe sample so we can measure where int8 impacts.
[00:08:29] Leah: We'll include token-diff histograms and also raw outputs for spot checks.
[00:08:33] Javier: Any concerns about security/compliance when toggling these runtime flags? We're in a tenant-isolated pilot but want to make sure logs don't leak PII in additional traces.
[00:08:42] Samir: Right — Priya, ensure trace redaction rules still apply. We won't enable full request body logging, only token-level metrics and hashed prefixes.
[00:08:52] Priya: Copy that. We'll use hashed prompt IDs.
[00:08:55] Maya: About the streaming rebuffer event we saw — can you capture the client-side event bucket so we can correlate network vs server?
[00:09:02] Leah: We'll add a client-side event header so the stream agent can include latency samples.
[00:09:06] Oliver: On the client side, we can also co-locate a tiny agent to simulate production pacing and provide synthetic load for the cohorts.
[00:09:12] Samir: Good. BluePeak, can you run the synthetic agent on one of your staging routes?
[00:09:17] Javier: Yes, we'll do that.
[00:09:19] Samir: Great. Quick recap: experiments, instrumentation, safety nets and expected deliverables.
[00:09:25] Leah: I'll drop the kernel.cfg and the runbook link to the shared drive after this call.
[00:09:30] Samir: Samir to follow up on pricing impact estimate if int8 yields a 15% token cost improvement — short note to Javier.
[00:09:36] Javier: Sounds good.
[00:09:38] Maya: Anything else on metrics?
[00:09:40] Priya: I think we're good. I'll push the dashboard changes and post links.
[00:09:44] Samir: Okay let's capture explicit next steps — (reads items).
[00:09:50] [00:09:50] (crosstalk: nods)
[00:10:02] Samir: Any blockers preventing experiments from starting tomorrow?
[00:10:06] Oliver: We need the sample prompts and the synthetic agent config from BluePeak, otherwise we can start toggling flags on low-traffic cohorts.
[00:10:13] Maya: We'll upload sample prompts by EOD tomorrow.
[00:10:17] Samir: Great. Last thing — schedule next check-in. Does next Tuesday 15:00 UTC work?
[00:10:23] Javier: Works for us.
[00:10:25] Samir: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[00:10:27] [00:10:27] (end of recorded portion)
